questions.question: Why is “trust” considered the ultimate product in insurance. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Insurance is a promise, not a physical product. The customer pays today for future compensation
  • they may never need — trust is what makes that promise credible. (1.5 Marks). Without confidence in
  • the insurer's reliability, claim settlement record, and financial strength, no customer will buy a policy.
  • Trust is therefore the core of the insurance relationship. (1.5 Marks)

questions.question: Examine how IRDAI contributes to the growth and development of insurance industry / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• IRDAI frames and enforces regulations on licensing, solvency margins, product approvals, and
  • agent conduct — ensuring the financial soundness of insurers and protecting policyholders from
  • malpractice (2 Marks) . By opening the market to private and foreign players (as JVs post -1999),
  • IRDAI fostered competition, product innovation (ULIPs, micro -insurance, health insurance), and
  • improved overall service quality (2 Marks) . IRDAI mandates grievance redressal mechanisms,
  • regulates claim settlement timelines, and runs public awareness cam paigns — building trust and
  • confidence in the insurance sector (2 Marks).

questions.question: The insurance marketing mix "focuses on building trust, clarity and accessibility." Explain how the elements of "Product" and "Price" specifically contribute to achieving this focus. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• In insurance, the product is an intangible policy — a promise of future compensation. Trust and
  • clarity are built through transparently worded policy documents with clear benefit s, exclusions, and
  • claim procedures. Relevant riders and add-on cover that address specific needs make the product more
  • meaningful and accessible to diverse customer segments (3 Marks) . Pricing must be perceived as
  • equitable to build trust. Competitive and fair premiums, flexible payment modes (monthly, quarterly,
  • annual), and discount mechanisms like NCB (No Claim Bonus) make insurance financially accessible.
  • Transparent premium calculation — explaining how age, health, and coverage affect cost — reassures
  • customers and reinforces confidence in the insurer (3 Marks).

questions.question: Discuss the scope of market research. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Any 4 of the following (1.5 marks each):
  • • Consumer Research: Studying policyholder behaviour, needs, preferences, and satisfaction
  • levels to design better products and target communication effectively.
  • • Product Research: Identifying gaps in existing insurance offerings and developing new
  • products for emerging risks (e.g., cyber insurance, parametric insurance).
  • • Market Analysis: Assessing market size, growth trends, competitive landscape, and the impact
  • of regulatory changes to inform strategic planning.
  • • Distribution Research: Evaluating the performance of different channels (agents,

questions.question: Describe ULIPs and their features. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• A ULIP (Unit Linked Insurance Plan) is a hybrid financial product that combines life insurance
  • protection with market-linked investment, regulated by IRDAI with a mandatory 5-year lock-in period
  • (Definition :2 Marks)
  • Key Features (1 mark each, any 4):
  • • Dual Benefit: Provides both a death benefit (life cover) and returns from market -linked
  • fund performance.
  • • Fund Choice: Policyholders choose from equity, debt, or balanced funds based on their risk
  • appetite, and can switch between funds.
  • • Transparency: NAV (Net Asset Value) is declared daily; all charges (mortality, admin, fund
  • management) are disclosed upfront.
  • • Flexibility: Allows partial withdrawals, top-up premiums, and fund switching after the 5 -
  • year lock-in period.
  • • Tax Benefits: Premiums qualify for deduction under Section 80C; maturity proceeds are
  • exempt under Section 10(10D) of the Income Tax Act.

questions.question: Explain underwriting guidelines and their importance in insurance operations. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• Underwriting guidelines are a standardized set of rules and criteria established by an insurance
  • company to ensure consistency, fairness, and discipline in risk assessment and policy acceptance
  • decisions across all applicants (Definition :2 Marks).
  • Key Guidelines Include:
  • • Age and health limits for acceptance of proposals.
  • • Premium loading (extra charge) for substandard or high-risk individuals.
  • • Mandatory medical examinations above specified sum assured thresholds.
  • • Exclusions for pre-existing medical conditions.
  • Importance (4 Marks):
  • • Consistency: Ensures all applicants are evaluated on uniform parameters, preventing bias or
  • arbitrary decisions.
  • • Prevents Adverse Selection: Stops only high -risk individuals from purchasing coverage,
  • protecting the insurer's risk pool.
  • • Financial Solvency: Avoids excessive risk concentration that could threaten the insurer's ability
  • to pay claims.
  • • Policyholder Protection: Sustainable underwriting keeps premiums viable and ensures long -
  • term claim-paying capacity.

questions.question: Explain the evolution of insurance industry in India. / [CO1] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Pre-Independence Era (2 Marks): Life insurance began in 1818 with the Oriental Life Insurance
  • Company, primarily serving Europeans. Indian lives wer e charged higher premiums. The Bombay
  • Mutual Life Assurance Society (1870) was the first Indian -owned company to insure Indian lives at
  • standard rates. The Insurance Act of 1938 introduced basic regulatory oversight.
  • Post-Independence & Nationalization (2 Marks): LIC was established in 1956 by nationalizing
  • all private life insurers, creating a state monopoly focused on spreading insurance awareness
  • to rural India and channelling savings into national development. General Insurance
  • Corporation (GIC) was formed in 1972 for non-life insurance.
  • Liberalization & Modern Era (2 Marks): The Malhotra Committee (1993) recommended
  • sweeping reforms; IRDAI was established in 1999, ending state monopolies and allowing
  • private and foreign players (as joint ventures). This triggered product innovation, improved
  • service quality, and rapid premium growth. Digital channels and InsurTech (AI, big data,
  • mobile apps) have further transformed the industry in the 21st century.
